title: Designing a REST API
summary: Designing a REST API is modeling the domain as plural resources, with predictable routes, filters, pagination and versioning.

sections.definition: Designing a REST API is modeling the domain as resources (plural nouns), with predictable routes, relationships expressed with moderate nesting, filters and ordering in the query string, pagination for collections and a versioning strategy from day one.
sections.analogy: An airport signage system: consistent names ("Gates A1–A20"), a clear hierarchy ("Terminal 2 → Gate B5"), no signs saying "Walk-to-the-plane-now". If each terminal used different conventions, nobody would make their flight.
sections.problem: A badly designed API is hard to learn, to document and to evolve without breaking clients. Offset pagination (?page=3) is simple and lets you jump to a page, but it gets slow with large tables and repeats or skips items when data is inserted. Cursor pagination is stable and fast, but it does not let you jump to page 50. Versioning in the URL (/v1) is the most common and visible; by header it is more "pure" but less practical.

sections.bridge:typescript: A paginated table works with offset because it needs to jump between pages and show the total. An infinite scroll, on the other hand, fits cursor. When you design the API for your own frontend, choose the pagination according to the UI.
sections.interview: I model the domain as resources with plural nouns, for example /clientes, /pedidos and /productos, and let the HTTP method express the action. I use one level of nesting for ownership relationships, like /clientes/7/pedidos, and direct access for everything else. Filters, ordering and pagination go in the query string. To paginate I choose offset when the UI needs to jump between pages and the table is moderate, and cursor when there is a lot of volume or changing data, because it is stable and efficient. I version from the start, usually in the URL as /v1, and only bump the version for incompatible changes. Actions that are not CRUD I model as sub-resources, for example POST /pedidos/1093/cancelacion.
sections.myths:
• Mixing singular and plural (/cliente/7 and /pedidos). The convention is always plural.
  • Believing every relationship must be nested. More than one level usually means the resource deserves its own route.
  • Breaking contracts without versioning: renaming a field is an incompatible change.

exercises.prompt: Review this design: is each endpoint correct or does it have an error?

items.why: Correct: plural resource and an id.
Verb in the URL. It should be POST /v1/pedidos.
Correct: filter in the query string.
GET with a side effect and a verb in the path. It should be DELETE /v1/pedidos/1093.
Mixes singulars and does not say which order. It should be /v1/clientes/7/pedidos.
Correct: creates a payment as a sub-resource of the order.
Technically valid, but with offset at that depth the query is expensive. On large tables, cursor.
